text: A stage tells Snowflake where a file lives. A file format tells it exactly how that file is shaped — so COPY INTO knows how to read it.

You define a file format once, by name, and reuse it everywhere. This CREATE FILE FORMAT statement is running in a real worksheet, and that one line handles quoted fields — the classic case where a comma sits inside the text itself.

SHOW FILE FORMATS proves it stuck. Same worksheet, and you can see the stage from the last lesson still sitting in the object tree on the left — a reminder that stages and file formats are separate, permanent objects.
File formats aren't global. They belong to a database and a schema, exactly like tables do, so set your context before you create one.
For CSV, a few options matter most: the delimiter, whether to skip a header row, how quoted fields are enclosed, and which strings should be treated as NULL.
JSON needs almost nothing beyond its type and whether to strip an outer array. Parquet needs even less — it carries its own schema, so there's nothing to configure.
Next: COPY INTO itself — the command every stage and file format exists to serve.
